**The Country of Night**

There was a time when night was not merely the absence of day but a place people traveled to—a country with its own customs, its own economy, its own strange hospitality. We have mostly forgotten how to visit it. We dim our screens, close our curtains, and treat the dark as a problem to be managed rather than a destination. But for most of human history, night was where half of life happened, and the people who lived then knew it in ways we can barely reconstruct.

The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through court records, diaries, letters, and medical texts from the centuries before electric light, looking for evidence of how people actually slept. What he found unsettled the modern assumption that a full night's rest is one unbroken block. Again and again, across cultures and centuries, he found references to "first sleep" and "second sleep." People went to bed a few hours after dusk, slept deeply, and then woke naturally around midnight. For an hour or two they were simply awake. They prayed. They talked with family. They visited neighbors by moonlight, smoked, read, made love—physicians of the era considered the interval ideal for conception—or did small chores. Then they returned to bed and slept until dawn. The gap between the two sleeps had names: "the watch," "the waking." It was so ordinary that nobody thought to explain it, which is why it took a historian to notice it had vanished.

And vanish it did. As artificial light spread through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the two sleeps collapsed into one. Ekirch has suggested that some modern insomnia may be a kind of ancestral echo: a person wakes at two in the morning, expects to fall straight back asleep, fails, panics—and the panic itself is what keeps them awake. Their body may be doing exactly what bodies did for millennia. The failure is not biological but historical. They are trying to sleep like moderns while their nervous system keeps old hours.

Before the lamps, night was genuinely dark in a way almost no one alive today has experienced. After moonset, a road between villages was a black corridor. People timed their journeys by the phase of the moon. Curfews rang from church bells; city gates swung shut; watchmen called out the hours into streets where anything might be moving. And yet the darkness was also a kind of commons. It belonged to no one, which meant it belonged to anyone bold enough to use it. Smugglers ran their cargo. Poachers filled their sacks. Lovers slipped out of houses. Debtors disappeared. The powerful hated the dark precisely because they could not see into it, and the powerless loved it for the same reason.

Then the light came, and it came first as policy. In 1667, Paris decreed that lanterns be installed throughout the city and that residents hang candles at their windows at the first sign of trouble. Other capitals followed. Gaslight arrived in the early 1800s and did something stranger than illuminate: it extended the working day indefinitely, turning night into a suburb of commerce. Shop windows glowed. Factories ran shifts. The evening became an economic zone. Electricity finished the job. By the twentieth century, night had been annexed—patrolled, metered, scheduled. The old country still existed, but you needed a passport most people no longer carried: a willingness to be afraid, or at least to be uncertain.

We tell ourselves this was all gain, and much of it was. Streets grew safer. Study became possible for people who labored by day. But something was traded away, and we rarely itemize it. In 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, and in the days that followed, observatories and police stations reportedly received calls from residents worried about a vast, glittering cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. Many callers had never seen it. Today, because of light pollution, roughly a third of humanity—including most people in Europe and North America—cannot see the galaxy we live inside. It hangs above us every clear night, and we have erased it the way you erase a single word, without quite noticing that the sentence changed.

The losses are not only aesthetic. On beaches edged by development, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the sand and crawl toward the streetlights instead of the ocean, toward whatever shines brightest, and die there. Migrating birds, drawn off course by the glow of cities, circle illuminated towers until they drop. Moths—pollinators, food for bats and songbirds—spiral into porch lights and spend their brief lives in confusion. Darkness is not emptiness. It is infrastructure. Whole economies of the living run on it, and we have been quietly bankrupting them for a century, one floodlit parking lot at a time.

And yet the old country has not surrendered entirely. It survives in pockets and in people. It survives in the night nurse walking a quiet ward, the baker firing ovens at three, the long-haul driver watching the horizon turn gray. It survives in the insomniac at the kitchen table, who occupies, without meaning to, the same hour her ancestors kept as the watch. There is a reason so many honest sentences get written at that hour. The mind at three in the morning is less defended. The usual committees have gone home. Whatever is true in you stands closer to the surface, the way fish rise in the dark.

If you want to visit what remains, it is not difficult. Wait for a new moon. Drive past the last streetlight, farther than seems reasonable, and stop somewhere the road forgets you. Get out. Give your eyes twenty minutes—they need that long to open fully, an adjustment our ancestors made nightly and we almost never make at all. Then look up. The dark will still be there, patient, indifferent to our schedules, holding everything we have forgotten in plain sight.

The old country still existed, but you needed a passport most people no longer carried: a willingness to be afraid, or at least to be uncertain.

We tell ourselves this was all gain, and much of it was. Streets grew safer. Study became possible for people who worked by day. But something was traded away, and we rarely itemize it. In 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, and in the days that followed, observatories and police stations reportedly received calls from residents worried about a vast, glittering cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. Many callers had never seen it. Today, because of light pollution, roughly a third of humanity — including most people in Europe and North America — cannot see the galaxy we live inside. It hangs above us every clear night, and we have erased it the way you erase a word, without ever quite noticing the sentence changed.

The losses are not only aesthetic. On beaches lit by development, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the sand and crawl toward the streetlights instead of the ocean, toward the brightest thing, and die there. Migrating birds, navigating by stars they can no longer see, circle illuminated towers until they drop. Moths — pollinators, food for bats and songbirds — spiral into porch lights and burn out their brief lives in confusion. Darkness is not emptiness. It is infrastructure. Whole economies of the living run on it, and we have been quietly bankrupting them for a century, one floodlit parking lot at a time.

And yet the old country has not surrendered entirely. It survives in pockets and in people. It survives in the night nurse walking a quiet ward, the baker starting ovens at three, the long-haul driver watching the horizon turn gray. It survives in the insomniac at the kitchen table, who occupies, without meaning to, the same hour her ancestors kept as the watch. There is a reason so many honest sentences get written at that hour. The mind at three in the morning is less defended. The usual committees have gone home. Whatever is true in you tends to stand closer to the surface, the way fish rise in the dark.

If you want to visit what remains, it is not difficult. Wait for a new moon. Drive past the last streetlight, farther than seems reasonable, and stop somewhere the road forgets you. Get out. Give your eyes twenty minutes — they need that long to open fully, an adjustment our ancestors made nightly and we almost never make at all. Then look up. The dark will still be there, patient, indifferent to our schedules, holding everything we've forgotten in plain sight.
